title: The Starry Night
summary: The Starry Night is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter Vincent van Gogh. Painted in June 1889, it depicts the view from the east-facing window of his asylum room at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, just before sunrise, with the addition of an imaginary village. It has been in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York City since 1941, acquired through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest. Described as a "touchstone of modern art", The Starry Night has been regarded as one of the most recognizable paintings in the Western canon.

sections.name: the swirling sky
sections.description: The dominant feature of the painting, featuring stylized blue swirls and luminous yellow stars. It represents the turbulent emotional energy Van Gogh perceived in the night sky.

sections.name: the crescent moon
sections.description: A bright, glowing orange-yellow crescent moon in the top right corner. It is a focal point of light and warmth against the cool tones of the night.

sections.name: the morning star
sections.description: The largest, brightest white star to the right of the cypress is identified as Venus, which Van Gogh referred to as the 'morning star' in his letters.

sections.name: the cypress tree
sections.description: A tall, dark, flame-like cypress tree on the left. In the late 19th century, these trees were symbols of mourning and mortality, providing a somber balance to the sky.

sections.name: the village
sections.description: A peaceful, imaginary village nestled in the valley, featuring dark houses with glowing windows and a prominent church spire.

sections.name: the church spire
sections.description: The tall, slender spire of the village church reaches upward, echoing the verticality of the cypress tree and reflecting Van Gogh's Dutch heritage.

museum_facts: Van Gogh painted this oil on canvas in June 1889 while staying at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in Saint-Rémy.
The sky is dominated by a bright moon on the right and Venus near the center-left.
Though inspired by the view from his asylum window, the village came from other views, and the cypress is shown much closer than it was.
Van Gogh painted this nighttime scene in several sessions during the day, using vivid blues and yellows to heighten its expressive mood.

guide_notes.the swirling sky: The raised line is a spiral: follow it from the outside and it winds in toward the middle, like the great swirl in the sky. Van Gogh built the sky from thick, short brushstrokes of ultramarine and cobalt blue.
guide_notes.the crescent moon: The moon is the upright crescent on the left of the board, curved like the letter C and open to the right. Records show the real moon that June was nearly full, so Van Gogh painted it as a crescent on purpose.
guide_notes.the morning star: The star is a set of rings, one inside another, with a small raised block at the very center: a bright star with halos of light around it. Van Gogh wrote to his brother Theo that before sunrise he had seen the countryside with nothing but the morning star, which looked very big; it is usually thought to be Venus.
guide_notes.the cypress tree: The cypress is the tall flame outline, a single point at the top widening down to a flat base along the bottom row. Van Gogh admired cypresses for their lines and compared their proportions to an Egyptian obelisk.
guide_notes.the village: On the left, a thin line rises from the top into a thicker tower: that is the church. Below and to the right are the outlines of houses, and the bottom row is the ground. Van Gogh could not see this village from his window; he added it from imagination.
guide_notes.the church spire: A single raised line at the top widens into a tall pointed tower, with its base along the bottom row. The steeple looks more like a Dutch church from Van Gogh's childhood than one in Provence.
